commentary.bottom_line: One retrospective study found that clinicians' decisions to use AI-drafted text tracked closely with automated quality metrics, which suggests logged dispositions may carry usable signal, but no study has tested whether monitoring override, edit, or reliance rates improves combined human-AI performance. Seven hazard studies show that over-reliance, non-adherence, and undocumented overrides occur in real deployments.

perspectives.view: A single level 3 retrospective replay study tests one part of the practice. It reports that clinicians' use of AI drafts correlated with quantitative metrics. The study measures agreement rather than patient outcomes or changes in combined performance after monitoring began, and it gives no effect size. Indirectness and imprecision place certainty at very low.

In one sepsis program, only 28% (555/1977) of huddles occurred without an alert firing, which suggests clinicians may defer to the alert. In surgery, four of five post-implementation errors occurred in cases where AI authentication was not used. These studies show that reliance and disuse both carry harm, but none shows that monitoring these rates catches errors earlier.

Physicians changed a median 9.0% (IQR 2.5%-21.9%) of AI note words, left 14.9% (143/960) of notes unedited, and averaged between 1.9% and 69.3% edits individually. About a third of physicians did not follow a UTI recommendation tool. This spread suggests clinician-level baselines may be needed before edit or override rates can be read as reliance signals.

A study in the United States that included patients with limited English proficiency found that clinician launches of a prediction screen did not differ by race, ethnicity, or primary language. In Israel, physicians in the Arabic sector were less likely to follow recommendations (OR 3.474). Disposition logs stratified by patient and clinician group could detect such differences, though no study has tested this.

Intensive care nurses in one qualitative study (n=23) described overriding early warning alerts without documentation under workload pressure. This suggests override logs that depend on manual entry may undercount overrides where staffing is tight. The draft-use study suggests automated metrics could reduce human review effort, though no study reported staffing needs or costs.

commentary.research_gap: No study has compared units that monitor disposition, override, and edit rates with units that do not, using combined human-AI accuracy, missed diagnoses, or patient harm as outcomes. Studies also need to establish which override or edit rates signal over-reliance and which reflect appropriate skepticism for a given tool.
commentary.underserved_note: The one study that tests the practice did not report Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. A hazard study included patients with limited English proficiency and racial and ethnic minority patients, but it described usage patterns rather than testing monitoring, so health systems serving these groups have no direct evidence on whether disposition monitoring performs as intended for them.
